1:
How often Paul had actually stood in Corinth is the first question, and the catena cannot close it. Barnes holds that the phrase as if I were present the second time proves he had been with them only once, the visit recorded in Acts, and that a second had been resolved on and disappointed. Clarke lays out at length the contrary case of an earlier scholar, who dated a first stay of eighteen months from the year 52, a brief second visit in 55 that Luke passes over, and a third about 57; and then declines it as insufficiently evidenced. Ellicott sets the same two schemes side by side — three real visits, one of them unrecorded and without any trace, or one real, one abandoned and one now intended — and prefers the second as fitting the known facts. Robertson will not decide: the participle may mean as when he was present a second time, which assumes the visit was made, or as if present, and the word again in the next clause settles nothing either way. Gill offers two reckonings, one counting the letters as comings, the other a visit, a prevented purpose and the present intention. Henry reports both readings without choosing, and turns to the tally itself: Paul kept account of how often he had taken pains with them, and an account is kept in heaven of the helps we have had. Wesley states flatly that he had been coming twice before though he did not actually come; Calvin reckons the year and a half in Acts as the one visit.

The rule about two or three witnesses divides them more sharply. Chrysostom takes Paul to be setting his comings and his warnings in the place of witnesses, joining the unwritten to the written, and observes that he has diverted a text from its first application before now, as when he used words spoken of lawful marriage against the man joined to a harlot — here too, to terrify them the more. Calvin says the same thing in his own terms: the quotation is not made in the natural and literal sense but by accommodation, and the threefold effort for their welfare may fairly stand for three persons. Henry finds the two epistles to be the witnesses, and thinks the allusion is rather to our Lord’s rule of dealing with an offender than to the law of Moses about judges. Gill counts three witnesses together with a first and second admonition. Against all of these Ellicott insists there is no adequate reason for refusing the words their simple and natural meaning as an axiom of Jewish and almost of natural law: to catch at the accidental juxtaposition of the third time and the three witnesses is strained and almost fantastic, and open to a fatal objection, since it turns the judge into a prosecutor and makes him cite his own repeated charges as evidence of their truth. He names no one, though the reading he demolishes stands a few lines away in this same collection.

On the threat itself there is more agreement. Chrysostom admires the wisdom and tenderness of a man abundant in admonition but slow to punish, who warns and warns again and holds the blow suspended, in this imitating the God who threatens often and chastises seldom. Calvin makes the same contrast a rule for pastors: mildness where it is safe, severity where necessity requires, since nothing is more hurtful than excessive indulgence; and he defends naming individual offenders on the ground that these sins were notorious. Barnes recalls the taunt that Paul was bold to threaten and afraid to execute. Clarke and Ellicott both understand the punishment concretely, as the sentence of excommunication and delivery to Satan, which Clarke takes to have carried a real power of inflicting bodily harm. Wesley extends it to any who have sinned since in these kinds.
3:
Gill sets out what the demand amounted to: they had queried whether Paul was sent by Christ, whether the gospel he preached was Christ’s voice, and whether he really had the power to punish that he threatened — a strange infatuation, since they themselves were the seals of his apostleship. Clarke makes the same point in one stroke: their own conversion was a solid proof that Christ spoke by him. Barnes answers the demand differently, holding that the proof would be furnished in the punishment itself, and reads the clause about Christ not being weak toward them as pointing to the diseases and calamities they had already suffered for their disorders rather than to miracles; the connexion, he thinks, requires it. Ellicott hears a touch of indignant sadness, and observes that men who feel that might all too keenly will not reproach Him with weakness. Robertson says only that Paul will give the proof asked.

Calvin turns the verse into a question about authority itself. He mentions that earlier expositors read it as Paul submitting himself to trial, but prefers to take it as a warning that the injury falls on Christ: when Paul’s admonitions are despised, Christ’s patience is tried. Then he raises an objection against himself. Will a man’s doctrine be exempt from all investigation as soon as he boasts that Christ is his authority? What false prophet will not make that boast, and what then becomes of the command to try the spirits whether they are of God? His answer is that Paul does not merely claim it but proves it, since Christ had already wrought efficaciously among them through his ministry. From this Calvin draws a rule: whoever speaks in the Church, whatever title he claims, may lawfully be examined as to his doctrine until Christ has manifested Himself in him — and only when it is plain that the word of God is being advanced does unbelief become unbelief toward God.

On the crucifixion through weakness, three of them press the voluntariness of the death. Gill argues that as God Christ could have prevented it, and instances the men struck to the ground at his apprehension and the word to Pilate that he could have no power except from above; the crucifixion was not owing to any want of power as God, but he became capable of it through his weakness as man. Clarke says none could take his life from him, and that he might have had twelve legions of angels — but then how could the Scripture be fulfilled? Barnes settles on the human nature and the appearance of weakness: Christ did not choose to exert his power, offered no resistance, and bore a nature peculiarly sensitive to suffering. Calvin agrees that the weakness names Christ’s humanity and the power his divinity, but then attacks a version of the voluntariness argument directly. It is right, he says, that Christ suffered by appointment and not by constraint; but some wrongly extend that appointment to his human will, as though dying were a permission contrary to his nature rather than the condition of it. He died because he chose to; yet that choice came of his having clothed himself with a mortal nature, and if we make his humanity so unlike ours the main support of our faith is overturned. Ellicott notes that the better manuscripts drop the concessive and read simply that He too was crucified, making Christ the highest instance of the law that strength is perfected in weakness; and he insists that the promise we shall live with him refers to the spiritual power now exercised for their good, so that to read it of the future resurrection misses its force. Wesley reads it exactly the other way, as being raised from the dead, while taking the power of God to be the divine energy now in every believer.
5:
Ellicott shows how the command turns the tables: the pronoun stands before the verb in both clauses, so the stress falls on yourselves, and the sentence grows straight out of the demand two verses back. You seek a test of my power; apply a test to yourselves. Barnes distinguishes the two verbs, the first a general scrutiny and the second the stronger word used of assaying metals by heat, and insists that the real proof is made in life rather than in reflection: a man who wants to know whether his axe is good does not sit and look at it, or read treatises on the properties of iron, but shoulders it and goes into the woods. Clarke works the same metallurgical figure to its end: try yourselves as you would try gold or silver suspected of adulteration, and take nothing for gospel that is not so, any more than you would take adulterated money for sterling coin. Gill divides the phrase, asking whether they stood in the doctrine of faith, holding it with an experimental knowledge, or in the grace of faith, which if genuine works by love. Calvin makes the self-examination a proof of Paul’s ministry rather than only of their state: since there is but one Christ, the same Christ dwells in minister and people alike, and if He dwells in the people He cannot be denied in the minister. A minister has a well grounded assurance of his doctrine only when he can appeal to the consciences of those he has taught; and from this Calvin draws the relation between preaching and faith, the one the mother that brings forth and the other the daughter that ought not to forget her origin.

The word rendered reprobates becomes the battleground. Clarke translates it base counterfeit coin, and says roundly that no other kind of reprobation is spoken of here than the rejection of adulterated metal; the adulteration came from the people themselves, for man pollutes himself and only then does God reprobate the polluted. Wesley says the word means such as cannot bear the test, and calls this its proper meaning. Ellicott defines it from the context as failing to pass the scrutiny, and adds that the ideas which Calvinistic theology has attached to the word are foreign to its true meaning here and elsewhere. Robertson observes that this is the very adjective Paul had held up before himself as a dreadful outcome to be avoided. Calvin is fighting a different battle on the same verse: against those who charge with rashness all who are persuaded that they are members of Christ, and would have believers content with a moral conjecture, he takes the question to establish the assurance of faith. Neither he nor Ellicott shows any sign of the other.

Wesley notes a rendering he does not adopt, that Christ is among you, understood of the miraculous gifts at work in the Corinthian church rather than of Christ indwelling each believer. On the following verse the tone softens. Gill says Paul would not pronounce whether they were reprobates, leaving that to themselves. Ellicott makes the pronoun emphatic: whether you fail the test or not, I hope you will know that we do not fail. Calvin presses the alternative hard — either they assign Paul the honour due to an apostle, or they condemn themselves for unbelief and confess they have no church — but notes that Paul softens it by hoping rather than asserting, and that in this second clause he says nothing of himself, putting their salvation in the place of his authority. Wesley puts it in a line: they shall know it by proving themselves, not by putting his authority to the proof. Robertson adds that the cure for vacillating Christians is to draw close to Christ, and Barnes and Clarke both expect the coming visit to furnish evidence enough of his commission.
7:
Gill and Ellicott both note that the weightier manuscripts read we pray. Henry takes the petition as the model of intercession: the most desirable thing we can ask for ourselves or our friends is to be kept from sin, and we are more concerned to pray that we may not do evil than that we may not suffer it. The faithful minister, he adds, wants the gospel honoured however his own person is vilified. Barnes reads the verse as softening what had just been said: Paul would rather lie under his enemies’ reproach of being no apostle at all than have them sin so as to give him the opportunity of proving that he is. Calvin makes it a maxim for the ministry: the pastor should be devoted wholly to the building up of the Church, and care for his own reputation only so far as it serves the common good. Clarke records a different construal, by which Paul asks that he himself may do them no evil, that is, may not be obliged to use the rod. Wesley and Robertson keep to the plain sense: Paul had far rather they did the noble thing.

The saying that they can do nothing against the truth is read three ways. Barnes and Clarke take it of apostolic integrity — commissioned men cannot teach a false doctrine or bend discipline to their own advantage, so the Corinthians need fear no severe handling. Gill turns it toward the readers: the apostolic authority was never meant for those who receive the truth in love, any more than the law is made for such persons. Ellicott finds the meaning below the surface: the condition on which that power is held is that it can never be used against the truth, so if they walk in it there will be no opening for its exercise, and he is content to seem to fail. He compares the wish to be accursed for his brethren and the Baptist’s willingness to decrease. Robertson takes the words as a general maxim: evil deeds can hold the truth down for a time, but in the long run the truth wins. Calvin makes the verse a limit on office, fixing the bounds of a pastor’s power, that he be a minister of the truth; and he turns it against those who quote he that heareth you heareth me to claim unbounded dominion while making war on the truth itself. Those who govern in the Church, he answers, are themselves subject to it. Henry reaches the same conclusion: the power given was for edification and not destruction, so Paul could not, would not and dared not act against it.

The last word of the ninth verse, which occurs only here, detains nearly all of them. Ellicott renders it restoration and traces the verb through the mending of nets; its proper meaning is to bring back to completeness, and this is what the apostle had been aiming at throughout, in his harshness as in his tenderness. Barnes carries the same sense of putting in order, and thinks Paul wished a reformation so entire that no discipline would be called for. Clarke takes the word for the setting of a dislocated limb, and quotes an earlier expositor to the effect that the members of this church were out of joint and needed rejointing in love; he applies it also to the soul, whose every faculty and appetite must be returned to its proper station. Calvin defines it as a fit proportion of all the members, and likens Paul to a physician who cures the disease without mutilating any part. Robertson remarks that Paul is no Jonah lamenting that Nineveh repented. Gill and Wesley say the apostles rejoiced when there was no occasion to exert their power, Wesley adding that the perfection wanted is in the faith that works by love.
10:
Chrysostom reads the verse as an explanation offered for the whole letter. Paul was sensible that he had spoken more vehemently than his custom, especially toward the end, and Chrysostom lists the places — the entreaty by the meekness of Christ, the readiness to avenge disobedience, the fear of finding them not such as he would, the warning that he will not spare — before giving the apology in Paul’s own voice: I would have the sharpness lie in my letters and not in my deeds; I wish my threats vehement, so that they may remain threats and never go into action. Yet even the apology, he observes, is made more terrible, since Paul points away from himself to the authority the Lord gave him. And he draws a further conclusion out of the closing words: if they continue unamended, then to punish men of that mind is itself a building up. Barnes takes the verse the same way as an apology for apparently harsh language, designed to prevent the necessity of severe measures on his arrival. Ellicott hears an inner conflict in which love has triumphed, not without pain; the storm has passed and the sky is clear again, and Paul neither recalls what he has written nor quite defends it, but explains and half apologises. It was better to speak with severity than to act; and even had action proved necessary, the aim would have been to restore them to their completeness in Christ, not to punish for punishment’s sake or to make a display of power.

Clarke and Robertson both fasten on the word rendered sharpness, which means a cutting off — a curt and abrupt dealing that occurs only here and in one other place in the New Testament. Clarke adds that the power was given rather to be employed in their edification than in their destruction. Gill takes the verse as the summary of everything Paul has done in writing: asserting his authority, showing his concern, desiring them to be kept from evil and set in a more orderly and comfortable condition before he arrives.

Calvin makes the clause about authority the point of the verse. Paul arms the strictness he has threatened with the authority of God, so that it may not seem thunder without lightning, or the excited onset of a man who has kindled himself without cause; he will not resort rashly to cruel remedies nor indulge his own passion, but simply execute the commission he was given. Calvin then notes that the words about building up and casting down are not used here as they were earlier in the epistle. There the gospel was commended from the advantage it yields; here the point is that although Paul might justly strike hard, it is far more his inclination to use his power for their edification, since that is its proper design. As the gospel is in its own nature the power of God to salvation and only by contingency a savour of death, so the authority given to its ministers ought to be salutary to those who hear, and if it turns out to their condemnation that is contrary to its nature. The meaning, he concludes, is that they should not through their own fault let what God appointed for salvation turn to their destruction; and by his example Paul admonishes all pastors how far the use of their power should extend.
11:
The parting word is the ordinary Greek greeting that means rejoice, and the commentators handle it differently. Ellicott says it was the natural close of a letter and is fairly rendered farewell if the fullness of its meaning is kept: let rejoicing be our last word to you. Clarke gives the English word an etymology, compounded from going and doing fairly, so that it means go on prosperously; and both he and Barnes add that this was among the dying Cyrus’s last words to his friends. Gill takes it as a call to spiritual joy in Christ — in his person, his righteousness, his blood and his fullness — and in the mercy of having so faithful a monitor.

Over the next word the catena splits along a doctrinal fault line. Clarke and Ellicott keep to the sense established two verses earlier: be compact, get into joint again, restore yourselves to completeness. Wesley reads it as a summons to the highest degree of holiness. Barnes turns aside into an argument. A command to be perfect, he insists, does not prove that it has ever in fact been obeyed, and an apostle’s wish that others might be perfect does not demonstrate that they were; the verse establishes an obligation and shows there is no natural obstacle, since God does not command impossibilities, but whether anyone besides Christ has been perfect is a question on which denominations have divided, and it lies with the advocates of sinless perfection to produce one instance of a perfectly sinless character — which, he says, has not been done. The demand and the doctrine it challenges stand a few lines apart, with no acknowledgment on either side.

The following exhortation is read as either a comfort or an admonition. Clarke observes that the verb covers begging, entreating and admonishing as well as consoling, and takes the harder sense: receive admonition, that ye may receive comfort. Barnes allows a reciprocal meaning, comfort one another, and reports a rendering that makes it the grateful receiving of admonition. Ellicott hears an echo of the letter’s opening chapter, and notes that the word for comfort and its verb occur twenty-eight times in this epistle, so that consolation is the keynote of the whole. Wesley says simply, filled with divine consolation.

On the call to one mind and to peace they largely agree, and the practical counsel is sharper than the exegesis. Henry would have them of one mind so far as possible, since the more easy we are with our brethren the more ease we have in our own souls; but where agreement in judgment cannot be had he presses the next thing, that difference of opinion should not alienate affection, and that debates, envyings and backbitings be avoided. Calvin makes the two commands distinct in kind: unity of mind concerns agreement of sentiment, peace concerns benevolence and the union of hearts, the second arising out of the first. Ellicott traces the phrase through Paul’s other letters and takes his thoughts to be travelling back to the old Corinthian schisms, as does Barnes. Clarke draws the negative conclusion with some force: love cannot live where there are brawls and divisions, and where neither peace nor love is found God cannot be, and if He is not there the assembly is made up of themselves and the devil. Calvin says the same more soberly, that where strife reigns the devil reigns. Henry ends on the promise: God is the author of peace and the lover of concord, and will dwell with those who live in love and peace here, and they with Him for ever. Calvin adds a word about the ending itself: Paul softens what has been sharp so as not to leave their minds exasperated, since reproofs profit only when seasoned with honey, and he seems here to turn from a few diseased members to the entire church.
12:
Ellicott begins with the tense of the verb, which he takes to show that Paul is directing a single act rather than instituting a usage: as the public reading of the letter came to an end, the men who had listened were to embrace and kiss one another in token that every offence was forgiven and nothing remained between them but peace. That the counsel was afterwards taken as a rubric he thinks natural enough, even at the cost of its becoming a stereotyped formula. He then follows it through the churches. An early order of discipline has the deacons call out the salutation and the clergy greet the bishop, the laymen the men and the women the women, with deacons watching that no disorder arose. In the earliest description of Christian worship the kiss comes before the offering of the bread and wine, as it did in most of the Eastern liturgies, probably in obedience to the command about leaving one’s gift at the altar; in the West it followed the consecration and the Lord’s Prayer. The African church left it out on Good Friday as unsuited to a day of mourning. When the Western church suppressed it altogether in the thirteenth century it was replaced by a carved tablet, passed from hand to hand and kissed in turn. Robertson supplies the same history from another angle. In the synagogues the sexes were separated and men kissed men and women women, and the Christian practice appears to have followed; it survives in the Coptic and Russian churches; and it was dropped because of the charges the pagans brought against Christians. He names the English archbishop who introduced the kissing board in the middle of the thirteenth century, and cannot resist the observation that a shared tablet is no improvement once one thinks of how disease is spread. Clarke does not enter the history at all and reads the command as practical counsel: use every means by which a good understanding may be brought about, and let the spirit of friendship live among you.

On the greeting from the saints the interest turns geographical and pastoral. Barnes and Clarke both take it of the believers with Paul in Macedonia, probably at Philippi, from where the letter was written. Clarke adds a remark about the word itself, that in the primitive church a saint and a Christian were the same thing, since the Christian religion calls every man to be holy. Ellicott notices the contrast with the first epistle, where the greeting came from the brethren of Asia and here from the saints of Philippi, and draws from it something about Paul’s habit: wherever he was, he told the church of one place that he was writing to another, and so made them feel that they all belonged to one family. Gill grounds the salutation in what the saints have in common rather than in where they are — the same divine favour, the same redeeming blood, the same sanctifying grace — from which follows a shared concern for one another’s welfare.
14:
Ellicott observes that the stormiest of Paul’s letters ends with the fullest benediction in the New Testament, taken early into the Eastern liturgies, though it reached its place in the English Prayer Book only in 1662. He makes something of the order of the names. Elsewhere the Father comes before the Son; here the sequence is reversed, as though for Paul there were no inequality between them and precedence were settled by the movement of thought — the grace declared sufficient for him, the love of God from which it flowed, and the fellowship by which both become experience. He treats the closing note about the letter being carried from Philippi as an unknown transcriber’s addition, without a shadow of authority, though probably a fair inference. Calvin confronts the same order: the love of God is the source of the grace of Christ, so the terms appear inverted. His answer is that Scripture speaks in two ways, telling us in one place that we were enemies reconciled by the death of the Son and in another that God so loved the world that He gave Him; in the first we look at ourselves, in the second at God. Viewed in Himself God loved us before the creation of the world; but we, finding in ourselves nothing but occasion of wrath, cannot apprehend that love without a Mediator, so that for us love begins with the grace of Christ. The fellowship of the Spirit is added because only under His guidance do we come to possess Christ at all.

Barnes treats the verse as a prayer with the optative understood, and draws three consequences: that worship may rightly be offered to the Son and the Spirit, since a prayer to God here is equally a prayer to them; that a real distinction exists in the divine nature, since it would be strange for an inspired man to ask in one breath for the grace of a man and the love of God; and that the Spirit is a person rather than an attribute, since prayer cannot be addressed to an attribute. Clarke reaches the same conclusion and expounds each title, the Lord who governs, the Jesus who saves by his passion, the Christ who distributes the divine unction. Then he presses the word for fellowship into an argument about assurance: can a man be a partaker with the Holy Ghost and not know it, and have the spirit of adoption by which he cries Father, yet know his relationship only by inference? Every genuine Christian who keeps a close walk with God may have as full an evidence of his acceptance as of his own existence, and any teaching that softens this by making the safest state consistent with endless doubts is a spurious gospel. Henry states the point briefly, that the verse acknowledges Father, Son and Spirit to be three distinct persons and yet one God, and that it fitly dismisses a worshipping assembly. Wesley agrees, and complains of those who leave before the sentence is finished.

Gill divides the first clause, taking the grace of Christ either for his love — one with the Father’s, as early and as endless, the ground of his becoming surety and dying in his people’s stead — or for the fulness lodged in him as Mediator, to be drawn from daily rather than exchanged for broken cisterns. Robertson calls it the most complete of the benedictions, presenting the persons of the Trinity in full form, and notes that Paul wrote such closing words with his own hand; by the time he reached Corinth the Judaizing trouble had gone, and the reading of this letter, he supposes, made a stir but did the work. Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse more narrowly, citing it at the end of a catalogue of Pauline texts assembled to prove that the Holy Ghost subsists, lives and speaks.
